transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I came in because something happened while I was working on a memorial piece for my aunt, and it really shook me more than I expected. I’m an artist, so I’m used to second-guessing choices—like, you know, whether a photo should be a little higher, or if a color feels too warm or too cold—but this felt different.

I kept getting these awful, unwanted thoughts that if I placed one photo wrong, or chose the wrong color, or made the piece not “right” somehow, then it meant I was dishonoring her. Like it would mean I didn’t love her enough, or that I was failing her memory. And I knew, on some level, that it didn’t really make sense—because it’s just an artistic choice, and I loved her—but I couldn’t just brush it off the way I normally can with creative doubts.

It kept sticking in my head, and it felt… intrusive, I guess. Like the thoughts weren’t something I wanted to be thinking, but they kept coming back and making me feel really distressed. That’s what made me think maybe I should talk to someone.

When you had those intrusive thoughts about dishonoring your aunt, did you feel driven to do something—like rearranging the photos, changing colors, or checking your work over and over—to try to reduce the distress or prevent something bad from happening?

Yes… yes, I did. It wasn’t like one dramatic ritual, exactly, but I’d get caught in these little loops that were really hard to stop.

Like I would reread the label text again and again, even if I’d already proofread it and knew it said what I wanted it to say. Or I’d nudge the same objects on the table—just a tiny bit to the left, then back to the right, then maybe rotate something slightly—trying to get this feeling that it was finally “settled.” And I kept checking the layout photos over and over, comparing them, zooming in, stepping back, taking another picture, looking at it again.

The frustrating part is that part of me knew it was already fine. I could see that nothing was actually wrong with it, but it didn’t feel okay yet, if that makes sense. So I’d keep doing it to calm down or make the thought quiet down, but then I’d lose so much studio time just trying to get back to that feeling of certainty.
Have these thoughts and the things you do to calm down taken up a lot of your time or made it hard for you to do things you need or want to do in your daily life?

Yes… I mean, I’m still functioning, mostly. I don’t want to make it sound like everything has fallen apart, because I am still getting most of my work done, and from the outside it probably looks like I’m just being very careful or particular in the studio.

But it is taking time. More than I want to admit, honestly. I’ll think I’m just going to check something for a minute, and then suddenly I’ve lost a big chunk of the afternoon adjusting and rechecking the same thing. And that’s not just annoying—it’s started to have consequences.

I actually missed a grant deadline because I lost so much studio time getting stuck on the memorial piece and then trying to catch up afterward. And I backed out of a gallery talk that I had really wanted to do, because I felt too tangled up and behind and couldn’t get myself organized enough to go through with it. So… yes, it’s mild in the sense that I’m not completely unable to work, but it’s definitely interfering.
